design_detail: Systematic review (24 studies) and multilevel random-effects meta-analysis (20 studies, 23 effect sizes) of cross-sectional comparisons between adults with a cocaine use disorder (DSM, ICD or equivalent criteria; by the inclusion criteria, current use or at most two months of abstinence) and control participants without cocaine use, on behavioural tasks of inhibition: stop-signal, go/no-go, Stroop, Five Digit Test, Immediate Memory Task, probabilistic reversal learning and the Attention Network Task. Hedges' g, positive for poorer inhibition in the cocaine group; dependence between effect sizes from the same study handled with an assumed correlation of 0.7 (0.0 to 0.8 in sensitivity analyses); metafor in R (estimator not stated); moderators by Q test and meta-regression; four publication-bias indicators on one effect per study; study quality by the JBI case-control checklist. PROSPERO CRD42024592030; PRISMA 2020; databases searched to January 2024.
can_establish: The average standardized difference on laboratory inhibition tasks between adults with cocaine use disorder and control participants across 20 small cross-sectional studies published up to January 2024, how widely it varies between studies, and how much it depends on a few studies.
cannot_establish: That cocaine use caused poorer inhibition (cross-sectional comparisons, unadjusted for the age and education differences the review itself documents, with a relation the authors call likely bidirectional), how large the difference is in any particular group (prediction interval −0.95 to 2.26), whether it changes with abstinence (study-level meta-regression across samples ranging from current use to about 11 months of abstinence), or whether inhibitory-control training helps (no training study was reviewed).

sample.recruitment: Search of Web of Science, Scopus and PubMed without date limits up to January 2024, English-language peer-reviewed articles (PDF p. 3). Primary samples were clinical (people seeking treatment from clinical services, detoxification programmes or rehabilitation centres) in 14 of the 24 studies and 12 of the 20 meta-analysed, and community (recruited through advertisements, flyers, newspapers or electronic media) in 10 and 8; 15 of the 24 studies were from the USA, the others from Spain, the UK, Belgium, Switzerland and Australia (PDF pp. 3, 11).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included: peer-reviewed English articles on cocaine use and cognitive inhibition in people aged 18 or older with a cocaine use disorder diagnosed by DSM, ICD (CIE) or equivalent criteria, with current use or at most two months of abstinence; a control group with no history of cocaine use; cross-sectional design; behavioural tasks of inhibition. Excluded: animal-only studies and imaging-only studies without behavioural tasks; other mental or neurodevelopmental disorders in both groups; another drug use disorder as first diagnosis; any drug use in controls except tobacco when both groups smoked (PDF p. 3). Of 38 full texts excluded, 19 had no healthy control group, 6 did not meet DSM criteria, 3 had an unknown main substance, 3 had drug use in controls and 2 did not assess inhibition; five were excluded for single other reasons, including methamphetamine use, heroin use and current psychiatric diagnoses in the cocaine group (Fig. 1, PDF p. 7).
sample.demographics: Meta-analysed samples (Table 2, PDF p. 8): 542 people with cocaine use disorder in groups of 11 to 55 and 656 controls in groups of 15 to 107; 78.97% men (two studies did not report sex); mean age 38.41 in the cocaine groups and 35.21 in controls (study means 28.18 to 52.6 and 28.6 to 42.66). By the editors' count, the cocaine group was 5 or more years older than its controls in 7 of the 19 studies reporting both ages. Years of regular use: study means 5.12 to 17.3 in 14 of the 20 meta-analysed studies (Table 1). Education, IQ and ethnicity are not tabulated.
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Four of the 24 reviewed studies did not enter the meta-analysis because their authors did not answer requests for data (PDF p. 3); by elimination from Tables 1 and 2 they are Kaufman et al. (2003), Torres et al. (2013), Van Der Plas et al. (2009) and Zilverstand et al. (2023), two reporting significant and two non-significant differences.
sample.selection_effects: English only, a full-text filter in PubMed, no grey-literature or reference-list search reported, and a printed PubMed string that omits one of the stated search terms (executive function) (PDF p. 3). Very small samples (median group sizes 22.5 with cocaine use disorder and 26.5 controls, editors' calculation from Table 2), mostly men, and frequent age and education differences between groups. The criterion of at most two months of abstinence was not applied as stated: five included studies report mean abstinence of 152 to 335 days (Table 1). Seven of the 24 included studies are missing from the reference list, so they cannot be identified unambiguously from the article.

exposure.measurement: Cocaine use disorder by DSM, ICD or equivalent criteria (inclusion criterion). Table 1 lists structured diagnostic interviews (mostly SCID) for most studies, but no clinical or diagnostic assessment (NA) for Hester & Garavan (2004), Kaufman et al. (2003) and Wang et al. (2018). Years of regular use and days of abstinence as reported by the primary studies; amount and route were not extracted. Two studies included people using cocaine and/or crack (Ceceli et al., 2023; Ersche et al., 2008).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Years of regular use: study means 5.12 to 17.3 (14 of the 20 meta-analysed studies; Table 1, PDF pp. 4–6). Amount, frequency and route: not extracted.
exposure.polysubstance: Table 1 lists current use of other drugs in the cocaine groups: alcohol 6.67% to 100%, cannabis 12.5% to 80%, heroin 3.7% to 33.34%, and amphetamines, opioids, hallucinogens, MDMA, benzodiazepines or polysubstance use (62% in Stevens et al., 2015) in some samples; only cocaine in 7 of the 24 studies; not determined in several. The two Verdejo-García studies are of cocaine and heroin polysubstance samples (reference titles). Co-occurring substance use could not be analysed as a moderator because most studies did not report it in detail (PDF p. 15). Controls: no drug use except tobacco where both groups smoked.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: By the inclusion criteria, current use or at most two months. Table 1 (means; PDF pp. 4–6): current use in four studies (Bjork et al., 2022; Ersche et al., 2008; Lane et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2011); 3 days in two (Hester et al., 2007; Hester & Garavan, 2004); 12.62, 13.5 and 21 days in three (Stevens et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2018; Vonmoos et al., 2013); 152 to 335 days in five (Verdejo-García & Pérez-García, 2007; Bell et al., 2014a; Ceceli et al., 2023; Bell et al., 2014b; Hester et al., 2013); not given for the rest. Zilverstand et al. (2023), in the review only, compared early (2 to 5 days) and longer-term abstinence. How abstinence was verified was not extracted.

comparison.controls: Control participants without a history of cocaine use and without other drug use except tobacco where both groups smoked; recruitment as in each primary study.
comparison.matching: Not required by the criteria. The review's own quality narrative reports group differences in education, age, sex or ethnicity, or inadequate matching, in 11 of the 24 studies (9 of the 20 meta-analysed), and Table 2 shows the cocaine groups 3.2 years older on average (38.41 vs 35.21); no pooled estimate is adjusted for these (PDF pp. 8, 14).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No included study measured inhibition before cocaine use (all cross-sectional). Pre-existing impulsivity, ADHD, education and IQ are not synthesized; the authors themselves state that inhibition may also influence cocaine use (PDF p. 15).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded except tobacco; the alcohol use of controls is not described.

outcomes.instruments: Stop-signal task (stop-signal reaction time; 10 of the 24 studies), go/no-go tasks (commission errors or no-go accuracy, including an error-awareness and a working-memory-load version; 8), Stroop (2), Five Digit Test (2), Immediate Memory Task (1), Probabilistic Reversal Learning (perseverative responses; 1) and the Attention Network Task (conflict effect; 1) (PDF pp. 11–12; Table 1).
outcomes.validity_norms: Experimental tasks without normative data; the authors state that clinical relevance therefore cannot be established (PDF p. 15). Study quality: JBI case-control checklist rated by the first author and an external collaborator, item kappas 0 to 0.5 (two not computable), converted to percentages (mean 89.06%) and labelled very low, low or moderate risk without stated thresholds (PDF pp. 9–11).
outcomes.operationalization: Poorer inhibition means a positive Hedges' g (the cocaine group's worse task score relative to controls). Different tasks and outcome variables are pooled as one construct, cognitive inhibition, which here also includes reversal learning, attentional conflict and impulsive responding; the variable taken from each study is shown only through Table 1's result column.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: One pooled outcome. Five moderator tests and four publication-bias indicators in three models were run without correction; all moderator tests were non-significant, so multiplicity does not change the conclusions.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable at review level; the external quality rater is described as blind to the review's objectives (PDF p. 11).

analysis.effect_sizes: Multilevel random-effects model, 23 effect sizes from 20 samples, within-study correlation assumed 0.7: g = 0.65 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.03), p < .001; Q = 134.26, I² = 83.61%; 95% prediction interval −0.95 to 2.26; aggregated model (one effect per study) the same; leave-one-out range 0.51 to 0.72 (PDF p. 12). Study-level g (Fig. 2, PDF p. 13): 18 studies between −0.55 and 1.20; Hester & Garavan (2004) 3.39, 3.92 and 4.90 (aggregated 3.56) and Lane et al. (2007) 3.13. Moderators: percentage of men Q(1) = 0.71, p = .401; years of use 0.21, p = .648; age 0.48, p = .488; days of abstinence 1.96, p = .162; clinical vs community 1.50, p = .220. Publication bias (one effect per study): fail-safe N 35; Begg 0.36, p = .028; Egger 3.00, p = .008; trim and fill one study; adjusted estimate not reported (Table 4). Editors' calculations (REML random effects on the 20 values printed in Fig. 2B, standard errors from the printed 95% CIs): this reproduces g = 0.65 (0.28 to 1.03) and the leave-one-out range 0.51 to 0.72, with τ about 0.80; without Hester & Garavan (2004) and Lane et al. (2007), g = 0.41 (0.20 to 0.62), I² about 65%, τ about 0.36, prediction interval about −0.39 to 1.21, and the classic Egger test is no longer significant (t = 1.05, p = 0.31; with all 20 studies t = 3.01, p = 0.007); clinical samples 0.45 (0.18 to 0.72), community samples 1.03 (0.07 to 1.99), community samples without the two outlying studies 0.32 (−0.04 to 0.68).
analysis.covariates: None at review level: the pooled effects are unadjusted group differences. Study-level meta-regressions on percentage of men, mean age, years of regular use and days of abstinence, and a Q test for clinical vs community samples; the number of studies in each meta-regression is not reported (at most 14 for years of use and for abstinence, by the editors' count of Table 1).
analysis.preregistration_detail: PROSPERO CRD42024592030; PRISMA 2020 (PDF p. 2). The registration date and any deviations from the protocol are not stated in the article, and the PROSPERO record was not read. The article's own abstinence criterion was not applied as stated (see reporting issues).
analysis.selective_reporting: τ is said to be computed but is not reported; the clinical and community subgroup estimates, the trim-and-fill-adjusted estimate and the number of studies in each meta-regression are not reported in the article (they may be in Supplementary Material 1, not read). The outlying effect sizes in Fig. 2 are not mentioned in the text.
analysis.power: Not formally addressed; the authors call the number of studies small and the samples low and ask for larger samples, especially in community studies (PDF pp. 14–15). Study-level meta-regressions on 20 or fewer studies have little power to detect moderation.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Across 20 small cross-sectional studies (542 people with cocaine use disorder, 656 controls), the cocaine groups performed worse on average on laboratory inhibition tasks (g = 0.65, 0.28 to 1.03), with high heterogeneity (I² 83.6%) and a prediction interval from −0.95 to 2.26. Two small studies with effects of 3.1 to 4.9 raise the average; without them the editors' recalculation gives 0.41 (0.20 to 0.62). Individually, 16 of 27 comparisons were significant (stop-signal reaction time: 4 of 10 studies). Funnel asymmetry was significant (Egger p = .008) and is no longer significant without the two outlying studies in the editors' reconstruction. No study-level moderator (sex, age, years of use, abstinence, sample type) was detected. The cocaine groups were older on average and, in about half the studies, differed from controls in age, education, sex or ethnicity without adjustment.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that the findings highlight the link between impaired inhibition and cocaine use disorder and suggest that inhibitory-control training would be promising, without the prediction interval or the publication-bias results (PDF p. 1). The third aim (PDF p. 2) and the conclusion frame the difference as an effect of cocaine ("cocaine use affecting inhibition as we observed in this study", PDF p. 15), although the same paragraph calls the relation likely bidirectional and the design is cross-sectional. The Discussion calls the studies of good quality with relatively low risk of bias (PDF p. 14) while the review's own appraisal lists unadjusted group differences in 11 of 24 studies; the funnel asymmetry is described as a small publication bias with no adjusted estimate (PDF pp. 13–15); a non-significant clinical-versus-community test is read as showing that training would suit both outpatient and in-treatment settings (PDF p. 14); null study-level meta-regressions are reported as showing that abstinence and years of use do not affect the estimate (PDF p. 14); the two outlying studies are not mentioned. Training itself was not studied, and the authors note that evidence on it is limited (PDF p. 15).

timeline.event: Jovanovski, Erb & Zakzanis quantitative review of neuropsychological tests in 15 studies: the most-studied inhibition-type measure there, Stroop Color-Word interference, had a mean d of −0.11 across 7 effect sizes; not cited by this review.
Spronk et al. comprehensive review of the cognitive effects of cocaine (to be appraised from its full text); not cited by this review.

Smith, Mattick, Jamadar & Iredale meta-analysis of behavioural inhibition (stop-signal and go/no-go tasks) across substances; as summarized by this review (PDF p. 15), it found inhibitory deficits with heavy use of or dependence on cocaine, MDMA, methamphetamine, tobacco and alcohol, and in pathological gambling.
Frazer et al. systematic critical review of long-term cognitive effects of cocaine (to be appraised from its full text); not cited by this review.

Rush et al. randomized pilot study of inhibitory-control training, with contingency management for clinic attendance, in cocaine use disorder; cited by this review as the limited evidence on training (PDF p. 15).
This review (published online 10 November 2025): g = 0.65 (0.28 to 1.03) across 20 studies to January 2024.

replication.where_it_stands: The most recent meta-analysis of behavioural inhibition in people with cocaine use disorder held by the project. It supports a cross-sectional difference in average task performance in the direction of poorer inhibition, of uncertain size (0.65 as published; about 0.41 without two outlying small studies by the editors' recalculation; prediction interval −0.95 to 2.26), and cannot show cause or reversibility. An earlier cross-substance meta-analysis (Smith et al., 2014) reached the same direction according to this review; the project's earlier neuropsychological reviews (Jovanovski et al., 2005; Spronk et al., 2013; Frazer et al., 2018) are not cited. The primary studies in Table 1 are inside the pooled estimate and must not be cited as independent support alongside it.

funding.funder: A García-Palmer grant from IdISBa granted to the first author (external internship agreement, annex number 2637; 08/01/2023–09/30/2023), as printed in the acknowledgements (PDF p. 15).
funding.declared_conflicts: All authors declare no conflict of interest (PDF p. 15).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the University of the Balearic Islands and the Health Research Institute of the Balearic Islands (IdISBa), the University of Oviedo and McMaster University's Peter Boris Centre for Addictions Research. None of the five authors is an author of the 17 included studies listed in the reference list; the other 7 included studies are not listed and cannot be checked. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A pre-registered, task-specific meta-analysis (stop-signal reaction time, go/no-go commission errors and Stroop interference analysed separately) with every effect size re-extracted and checked against the primary papers, restricted to samples matched on age and education or using adjusted estimates, and with abstinence measured and verified at testing; and, for the direction of effect, prospective cohorts that measure inhibition before regular cocaine use begins, or co-twin and sibling designs, with repeated testing during abstinence.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: PECO stated: adults with cocaine use disorder from clinical and community samples, cocaine or crack use, a control group, and inhibitory processing at the cognitive-behavioural level (PDF pp. 2–3).

PROSPERO CRD42024592030 and PRISMA 2020 are stated, but the registration date relative to the January 2024 search, the registered analysis plan and any deviations are not reported, and the record was not read. The article's own abstinence criterion was not applied as stated.
Cross-sectional designs were required without saying why; studies following people through abstinence, for example, are not discussed.

Three databases, no date limit, search terms and an example PubMed string (full strategies in Supplementary Material 1, not read); but English-only and full-text filters without justification, no grey literature, registries, reference lists or experts, a printed PubMed string that omits one stated term, and a search run 22 months before online publication. Judged no under AMSTAR 2 item 4 as written (unjustified language restriction), as for batch 3 cards; the senior author decides the project's reading (decision p-amstar2-item4).

Full texts were assessed independently by two reviewers (agreement 57 of 62, kappa 0.84), with a third author for uncertain cases; title and abstract screening is described as done by the same two reviewers, without saying whether independently (PDF p. 3).
No statement that data were extracted in duplicate or checked by a second person; the author contributions credit the first author with the review table and two other authors with the meta-analysis.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: Provisional: the article states that the 38 excluded full texts and the reasons for exclusion are listed in Supplementary Material 1 (Table 2), which was not read; Fig. 1 gives the reasons in aggregate. If the list is there, this item is met.

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Table 1 (country, sample type, concurrent drug use, years of use, days of abstinence, task, assessments, result) and Table 2 (group sizes, ages, sex); missing are the diagnostic method for three studies, education, the exact outcome variable used, and which group was used in studies with more than one cocaine group.

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: JBI case-control checklist covering comparability, matching, confounding and the measurement of exposure and outcome, rated by two people; but not selective reporting, low inter-rater agreement (item kappas 0 to 0.5), matching rated not applicable for the 10 studies classed as cross-sectional, and summary labels without stated thresholds that call studies low risk despite unadjusted group differences.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Multilevel random-effects pooling of Hedges' g with an assumed within-study correlation, sensitivity to that correlation, a prediction interval and leave-one-out analyses are appropriate techniques. But unadjusted group differences were pooled without justification although the review's own appraisal documents unadjusted age and education differences, conceptually different tasks were pooled without a task-level analysis, and effect sizes of 3.1 to 4.9 from two small studies were neither checked nor examined (the editors' recalculation shows they raise the estimate from about 0.41 to 0.65). The overall rating does not depend on this item.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: No subgroup or sensitivity analysis by quality score or risk of bias.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: The Discussion calls the studies of good quality and relatively low risk of bias and concludes that cocaine use affects inhibition, without considering the confounding by age and education that the review's own appraisal documents (PDF pp. 14–15).

Q, I² and a prediction interval are reported; heterogeneity was investigated with five moderators (none significant) and discussed as a limitation. Task type, named as a source of heterogeneity, was not tested and the two outlying studies were not discussed; judged met on balance.

Four indicators (fail-safe N, Begg, Egger, trim and fill), overall and by sample type, discussed as some or small publication bias (PDF pp. 13–15); but no adjusted estimate is reported and significant asymmetry (Egger p = .008) is called small. Judged met on balance.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Funding (IdISBa García-Palmer grant) and the absence of conflicts are declared (PDF p. 15).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Three critical items fail (4: restricted search; 11: unadjusted, mixed-task pooling without checking outlying effects; 13: a low-risk label and a causal conclusion despite documented confounding), so confidence is critically low by the AMSTAR 2 rule; item 7 is provisional (supplement not read) but cannot change the rating, which would stay critically low even if item 11 were judged met. The review has real strengths: registration, a PRISMA flow, duplicate full-text selection with agreement statistics, multilevel modelling, a prediction interval, publication-bias tests, and shared data and code. It may be cited for: a cross-sectional difference in average performance on laboratory inhibition tasks between adults with cocaine use disorder and controls (g = 0.65, 0.28 to 1.03), always with the prediction interval (−0.95 to 2.26) and the editors' sensitivity result (about 0.41 without two outlying small studies); and for the absence of detected moderation by study-level sex, age, years of use, abstinence or sample type, as an absence of evidence. It may not be cited for: cocaine causing poorer inhibition, recovery or its absence with abstinence, the included studies being at low risk of bias, or inhibitory-control training being effective.

key_findings.finding: Search of Web of Science, Scopus and PubMed without date limits to January 2024 (English; PubMed with full-text and human filters): 1725 records (922 Scopus, 715 PubMed, 88 Web of Science); 499 duplicates removed; 1226 titles and abstracts screened and 1164 excluded; 62 full texts assessed independently by two reviewers (agreement on 57, 91.9%, kappa 0.84); 38 excluded; 24 studies in the systematic review and 20 (23 effect sizes) in the meta-analysis. The authors of four studies were asked for data and did not respond.
key_findings.locator: Search Strategy, 1st paragraph; Selection and Data Collection Process, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; also Fig. 1 (PDF p. 7)

key_findings.finding: Inclusion: peer-reviewed English articles; people aged 18 or older with a cocaine use disorder by DSM, ICD (CIE) or equivalent criteria, with current use or at most two months of abstinence; a control group with no history of cocaine use; cross-sectional design; behavioural tasks of inhibition. Exclusion: other mental or neurodevelopmental disorders in both groups, another drug use disorder as first diagnosis, and drug use in controls other than tobacco when both groups smoked.

The meta-analysis pooled 542 people with cocaine use disorder (groups of 11 to 55) and 656 control participants (15 to 107); 78.97% men overall; mean age 38.41 in the cocaine groups and 35.21 in controls. Of the 20 meta-analysed studies, 12 used clinical and 8 community samples (14 and 10 of the 24 reviewed); 15 of the 24 were from the USA.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (PDF p. 8); Results › Study Characteristics, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (PDF p. 11)
key_findings.note: Editors' count from Table 2: the cocaine group was 5 or more years older than its controls in 7 of the 19 studies reporting both ages (largest gap 52.6 vs 36.4 years, Bjork et al., 2022).

key_findings.finding: Tasks across the 24 studies: stop-signal task 10, go/no-go 8, Stroop 2, Five Digit Test 2, Immediate Memory Task 1, Probabilistic Reversal Learning 1, Attention Network Task 1 (one study used two tasks).
key_findings.locator: Results › Inhibition Tasks Used in the Studies, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: Multilevel random-effects meta-analysis (23 effect sizes from 20 samples, within-study correlation assumed 0.7): g = 0.65 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.03), p < .001, poorer inhibition in the cocaine groups; heterogeneity Q = 134.26, I² = 83.61%, p < .001; 95% prediction interval −0.95 to 2.26. The aggregated model with one effect per study gave the same estimate, and leave-one-out estimates ranged from 0.51 to 0.72; other assumed correlations (0.0 to 0.8) gave similar results according to the authors (Supplementary Material 1, not read).
key_findings.locator: Abstract (PDF p. 1); Cocaine Use and its Impact on Inhibitory Control › Meta-analysis on the Relationship between Cocaine Use and Inhibitory Control, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 12)
key_findings.note: τ is said to be computed (PDF p. 8) but is not reported. Editors' calculation: REML random effects on the 20 study values printed in Fig. 2B, with standard errors from the printed confidence intervals, reproduces g = 0.65 (0.28 to 1.03) and the leave-one-out range 0.51 to 0.72, with τ about 0.80.

key_findings.finding: Study-level effects (Fig. 2): 21 of 23 positive; 18 studies lie between −0.55 (Vonmoos et al., 2013; 30 vs 68; 95% CI −0.99 to −0.12) and 1.20 (Stevens et al., 2015); two small community-sample studies lie far outside: Hester & Garavan (2004), three conditions of the same 15 vs 15 participants, g = 3.39, 3.92 and 4.90 (aggregated 3.56, 2.49 to 4.63), and Lane et al. (2007), 18 vs 15, g = 3.13 (2.11 to 4.15).
key_findings.note: Values read from the Fig. 2 image (no text layer) on a 300-dpi crop. Editors' calculation (REML on the Fig. 2B values): without these two studies g = 0.41 (0.20 to 0.62), I² about 65%, τ about 0.36, prediction interval about −0.39 to 1.21. For group differences of g = 3.1 to 4.9, about 94% to 99% of each group would lie on its own side of the midpoint under normal distributions.

key_findings.finding: No moderator was significant: percentage of men Q(1) = 0.71, p = .401; years of regular use Q(1) = 0.21, p = .648; mean age Q(1) = 0.48, p = .488; days of abstinence Q(1) = 1.96, p = .162; clinical vs community sample Q(1) = 1.50, p = .220 (printed as p < .220). Subgroup estimates and the number of studies in each meta-regression are not given in the article.
key_findings.locator: Meta-analysis on the Relationship between Cocaine Use and Inhibitory Control, 3rd paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation (REML on the Fig. 2B values): clinical samples g = 0.45 (0.18 to 0.72), community samples 1.03 (0.07 to 1.99), the latter 0.32 (−0.04 to 0.68) without the two outlying studies, both of which are community samples. Years of use and abstinence are available for at most 14 of the 20 studies in Table 1 (editors' count).

key_findings.finding: Publication bias, on one effect per study (k = 20): fail-safe N 35, Begg rank correlation 0.36 (p = .028), Egger test 3.00 (p = .008), trim and fill one missing study; clinical samples (k = 12): 17, 0.12 (p = .638), 1.11 (p = .294), none; community samples (k = 8): 2, 0.58 (p = .061), 2.45 (p = .050), one. The authors describe this as a small publication bias; no adjusted estimate is reported.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (PDF p. 13); Results › Publication Bias, 1st paragraph (PDF pp. 13–14)
key_findings.note: Editors' reconstruction (classic Egger regression on the Fig. 2B values): t = 3.01, p = 0.007 with all 20 studies, matching the printed result; without Hester & Garavan (2004) and Lane et al. (2007), t = 1.05, p = 0.31.

key_findings.finding: In the narrative synthesis, 16 of 27 comparisons across the 24 studies were significant: stop-signal reaction time was significantly longer in the cocaine group in 4 of 10 studies; go/no-go commission errors or accuracy differed in 5 of 8; the Attention Network Task, reversal-learning and Immediate Memory Task studies were significant; one of two Stroop and one of two Five Digit Test studies were significant. Of the 23 meta-analysed effects, 21 pointed to poorer performance in the cocaine group.
key_findings.locator: Systematic Review on the Relationship between Cocaine Use and Inhibitory Control, 1st to 5th paragraphs (PDF pp. 12–13); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 14)

key_findings.finding: Days of abstinence in Table 1 (study means): current use in four studies; 3 days in two; 12.62, 13.5 and 21 days in three; 152, 226.1, 293.23, 314.3 and 335 days in five (Verdejo-García & Pérez-García, 2007; Bell et al., 2014a; Ceceli et al., 2023; Bell et al., 2014b; Hester et al., 2013); not given for the others. The early-abstinence group of Zilverstand et al. (2023; review only) had 2 to 5 days.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, column Years of consumption (y) & days of abstinence (d)

key_findings.finding: Concurrent drug use in the cocaine groups (Table 1): alcohol 6.67% to 100%, cannabis 12.5% to 80%, heroin 3.7% to 33.34% (29.62% in Bell et al., 2014a, 25% in Bell et al., 2014b, 33.34% in Hester et al., 2013), with amphetamines, opioids, hallucinogens, MDMA and benzodiazepines in some samples; only cocaine in 7 of the 24 studies. The authors could not analyse co-occurring substance use or mental disorders because most studies did not report them in detail.
key_findings.locator: Table 1, column Comorbidity of current drug consumption (PDF pp. 4–6); Discussion, 4th paragraph (PDF p. 15)

key_findings.finding: Study quality (JBI case-control checklist; first author and an external collaborator; item kappas 0.47, 0.38, 0.45, 0.48, 0, 0.33 and 0.18 for items 1 to 7, not computable for items 8 and 9, and 0.5 for item 10): mean score 89.06%; 10 studies rated very low risk of bias, 13 low and 1 moderate. The review's own narrative reports group differences in education, age, sex or ethnicity, or inadequate matching, in 11 of the 24 studies, most of them rated low risk.
key_findings.locator: Table 3 (PDF pp. 9–10); Methods › Quality Assessment, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 11); Results › Methodological Quality of Included Studies, 2nd to 5th paragraphs (PDF p. 14)
key_findings.note: Editors' count from the narrative (PDF p. 14): Hester & Garavan (2004), Van Der Plas et al. (2009), Vonmoos et al. (2013), Bell et al. (2014a, 2014b), Elton et al. (2014), Liu et al. (2011), Wang et al. (2018), Albein-Urios et al. (2012), Lane et al. (2007) and Kaufman et al. (2003); 9 of them are in the meta-analysis.

key_findings.finding: Limitations stated by the authors: co-occurring substance use and mental disorders could not be analysed; some publication bias; few studies with small samples; high heterogeneity; experimental tasks without norms, so clinical relevance cannot be judged. Conclusion: people with cocaine use disorder have decreased inhibition compared with controls; the relation is likely bidirectional; inhibitory-control training is proposed as a target, with limited evidence so far (one pilot trial cited).

reporting_issues.issue: The inclusion criteria require current use or at most two months of abstinence (PDF p. 3), but Table 1 reports mean abstinence of 152 to 335 days in five included studies, all in the meta-analysis (Verdejo-García & Pérez-García, 2007; Bell et al., 2014a, 2014b; Ceceli et al., 2023; Hester et al., 2013).
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled estimate mixes current use with abstinence of up to 335 days, and the null abstinence meta-regression rests on study means across this mixed range. In an exploratory editors' calculation (REML on the Fig. 2B values), these five studies pool to g = 0.20 (−0.17 to 0.58) and the other 13, without the two outlying studies, to 0.48 (0.23 to 0.73); the comparison is post hoc and underpowered and cannot show recovery.

reporting_issues.issue: Two small studies have effect sizes far outside the rest that the text never mentions: Hester & Garavan (2004), 3.39, 3.92 and 4.90 from the same 15 vs 15 participants, and Lane et al. (2007), 3.13 (2.11 to 4.15). For Lane et al., Table 1 records the primary result as p = .019. By the editors' calculation from the t distribution, p = .019 with 18 vs 15 participants corresponds to d of about 0.87 if it is the same comparison, whereas g = 3.13 would correspond to p of about 4 × 10⁻¹⁰.
reporting_issues.consequence: The pooled g of 0.65, the high heterogeneity and the funnel asymmetry depend substantially on these two studies (editors' recalculation without them: g = 0.41, 0.20 to 0.62; Egger p = 0.31). Effects this large can arise when standard errors are taken for standard deviations or a different contrast is extracted; the primary papers or the review's OSF data would settle it.

reporting_issues.issue: For two studies, Table 1's record of the primary result does not match the review's own effect size: Hester et al. (2013) is recorded as significantly worse no-go accuracy (p < .05) but has g = 0.60 (−0.13 to 1.33) in Fig. 2; Vonmoos et al. (2013) is recorded as non-significant but has g = −0.55 (−0.99 to −0.12), a significant difference favouring the cocaine group. Vonmoos et al. studied recreational and dependent groups (Table 1), and which group was used is not stated.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either a different outcome, contrast or group was extracted, or there are extraction or sign errors; together with the outlying values, the effect-size extraction needs checking against the primary papers before the pooled value is relied on.

reporting_issues.issue: Seven of the 24 included studies are not in the reference list: Albein-Urios et al. (2012), Bell et al. (2014a, 2014b), Hester et al. (2013), Li et al. (2008), Torres et al. (2013) and Vonmoos et al. (2013); in Tables 1 to 3 their names carry no link to a reference.
reporting_issues.consequence: Six of the 20 meta-analysed studies cannot be identified unambiguously from the article (they may be identified in the supplement or OSF files, not read), which prevents checking their effect sizes, including the mismatches above.

reporting_issues.issue: The quality summary does not match the review's own observations: studies with unadjusted differences in education, age or sex are rated low risk (for example Elton et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2011; Lane et al., 2007); the matching item is rated not applicable for the 10 studies classed as cross-sectional, which lifts their scores to 100%; the thresholds for very low, low and moderate risk are not defined; item 4 (valid measurement of exposure) is rated yes for Hester & Garavan (2004), Kaufman et al. (2003) and Wang et al. (2018) although Table 1 lists no diagnostic assessment for them; and the text omits the kappa of 0 for item 5.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statement that the studies were of good quality and relatively low risk of bias (PDF p. 14) should not be repeated; confounding by age and education is unaddressed in about half of the studies.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion says clinical and community samples had similar years of regular use, both averaging 14.5 years, but by the editors' calculation from Table 1 the study means average 10.6 years for the 8 clinical and 13.2 years for the 6 community meta-analysed studies that report it (10.5 and 14.2 across all reviewed studies).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the argument that the two sample types were alike in duration of use is not supported as printed.

reporting_issues.issue: The stated search terms include executive function, but the printed PubMed string searches only inhibition, inhibitory control and impulsivity in titles and abstracts, with filters for full text, English and humans.
reporting_issues.consequence: Studies indexed under executive function without these words, and PubMed records without full-text links, may have been missed; the full strategies (Supplementary Material 1) were not read.

reporting_issues.issue: For studies with more than one cocaine group the group used is not stated (Vonmoos et al., 2013, recreational and dependent; Stevens et al., 2015, with and without ADHD), although use without a disorder and other mental disorders are excluded by the criteria; and studies with 25% to 33% concurrent heroin use and two cocaine and heroin polysubstance samples were included while one full text was excluded for heroin consumption (Fig. 1).
reporting_issues.consequence: It is unclear whether the pooled sample meets the stated criteria; if the ADHD subgroup was included, ADHD would confound the inhibition comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: The statement of the review's third aim and the sentence after it (PDF p. 2) follow, almost word for word by the editors' comparison, the statement of aims in Jovanovski et al. (2005, p. 191), which is not cited; nor are later reviews of cocaine and cognition held by the project (Spronk et al., 2013; Frazer et al., 2018).
reporting_issues.consequence: No effect on the results; the review does not compare its findings with the earlier quantitative review of the same literature.
